title: Quantifying the Necessity of Chain of Thought through Opaque Serial Depth
relevance_reason: Safety metric (circuit depth between interpretable nodes); analyzes autoregressive Transformers, RNNs, continuous CoT, diffusion, MoE, but not depth-looped Transformers.
one_sentence: Defines opaque serial depth as the circuit depth of computation between interpretable nodes, gives hand and automatic upper bounds for Gemma 3 and an MoE model, and asymptotic bounds for several architectures including continuous latent CoT.
key_contributions: Formal definition: depth of a network is the minimum depth of a poly(S)-size circuit computing it; opaque serial depth is the maximum depth between user-specified interpretable nodes (tokens).
Hand-calculated upper bounds for Gemma 3 1B-27B (4,490 to 11,662 at max sequence length) and an open-source JAX calculator that overestimates them by about 1.28x.

Asymptotic bounds: autoregressive Transformer O(L(log T + log D)), RNN O((L+T) log D), continuous latent CoT O(L T_cot (log T + log D)), black-box persistent memory unbounded; MoE likely lowers depth.

setup.model_sizes: Gemma 3 1B, 4B, 12B, 27B; vanilla MoE Transformer with 11.42B active / 91.32B total parameters (architecture only)

claims.claim: The authors state that adding recurrence should allow long serial cognition in activations, weakening the argument that thinking out loud is necessary, and suggest one may want to avoid recurrent architectures for monitorability.
claims.evidence_quote: For example, adding recurrence should enable long serial cognition within the activations, and so should reduce our expectation that thinking out loud is necessary.

claims.claim: Under the framework, continuous latent chain of thought composes the full network T_cot times, so its opaque serial depth scales linearly with the number of latent steps.
claims.evidence_quote: Assuming that we are using a Transformer architecture, each invocation of the 𝑓𝜃 has depth 𝑂 ( 𝐿 (log 𝑇 + log 𝐷)). Thus, the overall depth is 𝑂 ( 𝐿𝑇𝑐𝑜𝑡 (log 𝑇 + log 𝐷)).

claims.claim: For a standard autoregressive Transformer every token is interpretable, so opaque depth is limited to one forward pass: O(L(log T + log D)).
claims.evidence_quote: Thus, every layer has depth 𝑂 (log 𝑇 + log 𝐷). Since the overall forward pass is a composition of 𝐿 layers, the overall opaque serial depth is 𝑂 ( 𝐿 (log 𝑇 + log 𝐷)).

claims.claim: An MoE Transformer with 11B active parameters has a calculated depth well below dense Gemma 3 12B, suggesting MoE lowers serial depth.
claims.evidence_quote: The JAX calculator produces a depth of 4,096 for this model, which is significantly lower than the JAX-calculated depth of 11,268 for Gemma 3 12B, and even the by-hand calculation of 8,754 (Table 2)

numbers.what: By-hand opaque serial depth upper bound of Gemma 3 27B at max sequence length (formula 11322 + 20 log2 T)
numbers.quote: Final Depth Formula 4370 + 8 · log2 𝑇 6036 + 10 · log2 𝑇 8482 + 16 · log2 𝑇 11322 + 20 · log2 𝑇 Total Depth (T=T_max) 4,490 6,206 8,754 11,662

numbers.what: JAX calculator depth for an MoE Transformer (11B active / 91B total)
numbers.quote: The JAX calculator produces a depth of 4,096 for this model, which is significantly lower than the JAX-calculated depth of 11,268 for Gemma 3 12B, and even the by-hand calculation of 8,754 (Table 2)

numbers.what: JAX calculator overestimation vs hand calculation (Gemma 3 1B to 27B)
numbers.quote: By-Hand Depth 4,490 6,206 8,754 11,662 JAX Calculator Depth 5,728 7,958 11,268 14,856 JAX Overestimation 1.28× 1.28× 1.29× 1.27×

limitations: Requires a judgment about which nodes are interpretable; node-level interpretability is only one aspect of transparency; depth is a min over poly-size circuits so bounds are upper bounds only; JAX calculator supports a subset of operations. Depth-looped (weight-tied) Transformers are not analyzed.
survey_notes: SECTION: safety (Sec. 14, CoT monitorability paragraph). Statement 1: opaque serial depth is defined as circuit depth between interpretable nodes, and the authors themselves name recurrence as the change that would weaken the necessity argument: "adding recurrence should enable long serial cognition within the activations, and so should reduce our expectation that thinking out loud is necessary." Statement 2: for continuous latent CoT the bound is O(L T_cot (log T + log D)) ("Thus, the overall depth is O(L T_cot (log T + log D))"), versus O(L(log T + log D)) for a standard autoregressive Transformer; Gemma 3 27B has a hand bound of 11,662. CORRECTION for survey Sec. 14: the paper does NOT analyze depth-looped Transformers; its 'Recurrent Networks' case (Fig. 3b) is sequence-axis RNNs with O((L+T) log D). The survey sentence 'their opaque serial depth grows with the loop count by construction' is the survey's own derivation and should be labeled as such. Applying the paper's per-layer bound, a looped model running an L-layer block r times has opaque depth O(rL(log T + log D)): exactly that of an unshared model of the same effective depth rL, because circuit depth is implementation-independent (weight tying does not change it). So a fixed small loop count (e.g. r=4) is a constant-factor increase, not a qualitative change; only loop counts that grow with input or are unbounded at test time (convergence halting, test-time extrapolation) put looped models in the continuous-CoT regime. The MoE result (4,096 vs 11,268 for Gemma 3 12B) shows that architecture choices other than looping also move this metric.

title: A Pragmatic Way to Measure Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
relevance_reason: CoT monitorability metric for non-looped reasoning models; names latent-reasoning architectures as a threat but tests none.
one_sentence: Proposes legibility and coverage scores (0-4) computed by a prompted LLM autorater on correct CoTs for hard tasks, sanity-checks it with synthetic degradations, and finds five frontier reasoning models highly monitorable by default.
key_contributions: Two default-monitorability metrics: legibility (can a human follow the CoT) and coverage (does the CoT contain all reasoning needed to reach the output), scored only on correctly solved hard tasks.
A released autorater prompt validated on hand-crafted and synthetic degradations (Base64, Rot13, fictional language, removed steps).
Baseline: Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3 235B all score >= 95% on both metrics on HLE, GPQA, ARC AGI, AIME.

setup.model_sizes: Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3 235B (rated models); autorater Gemini 2.5 Pro (and Flash)
setup.benchmarks: Humanity's Last Exam, GPQA Diamond, ARC AGI, AIME

claims.claim: Monitorability can be lost through architectural change, explicitly including latent reasoning, so it must be measured to be preserved.
claims.evidence_quote: Shifts in training practices, such as scaled-up reinforcement learning, or the adoption of architectures that rely on latent reasoning, threaten to degrade or eliminate this visibility.

claims.claim: Current frontier reasoning models have high default legibility and coverage on difficult tasks.
claims.evidence_quote: All models achieve very high scores, indicating that their necessary reasoning is highly monitorable by default.

claims.claim: The metric measures default monitorability and does not replace adversarial stress-testing; it should not be used as a training objective.
claims.evidence_quote: To preserve the integrity of these measures, we do not recommend using them as a training objective, as doing so risks Goodhart's law.

numbers.what: Legibility and coverage (%) of Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3 235B
Legibility drop under legibility-targeted perturbations
numbers.quote: Perturbations designed to target Legibility result in Legibility scores dropping to values in the range of 0 to 50%, depending on the severity of the perturbation applied.

limitations: Preliminary prompt; not an adversarial stress test; does not measure faithfulness; depends on autorater capability; human-monitor lower bound only; only models with accessible internal CoT.
survey_notes: SECTION: safety (Sec. 14, monitorability measurement). Statement 1: a cheap, model-agnostic monitorability metric exists that the one looped-LM monitorability study (2610.02741, MonitorBench) did not use; it was designed so developers can track how 'architecture' choices affect monitorability: "the adoption of architectures that rely on latent reasoning, threaten to degrade or eliminate this visibility." Statement 2: non-looped frontier baselines are near ceiling (Legibility 97.33-99.94%, Coverage 95.27-99.38%, Table 1), so a looped model's coverage at increasing loop counts would be measured against a ceiling baseline; a coverage drop with more loops at fixed answer accuracy is the direct observable for computation moving out of the trace. The survey can propose this loop-count sweep as a concrete experiment (open problems P6). Caveat to state: the authors warn it measures default monitorability only and is "a complement, not a replacement" for stress tests. No correction to existing survey text; it is a missing citation for Sec. 14 and P6.

title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
relevance_reason: CoT faithfulness of non-looped reasoning models; baseline for whether visible CoT reflects single-forward-pass computation, which looping enlarges.
one_sentence: Measures how often reasoning models verbalize prompt hints they demonstrably use (6 hint types, MMLU and GPQA), finding low faithfulness, a low plateau under outcome-based RL, and almost no verbalization of learned reward hacks.
key_contributions: Hint-based faithfulness metric: among prompt pairs where adding a hint flips the answer to the hint, the fraction of CoTs that acknowledge the hint (noise-normalized).
Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1 verbalize used hints 25% and 39% of the time on average; less faithful on harder GPQA than MMLU.

Outcome-based RL raises faithfulness then plateaus (28% MMLU, 20% GPQA); in synthetic reward-hack environments the model exploits hacks on >99% of prompts but verbalizes them <2% of the time in 5 of 6 environments.

setup.model_sizes: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1 (reasoning); Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New), DeepSeek V3 (non-reasoning)
setup.benchmarks: MMLU and GPQA multiple-choice with 6 hint types; synthetic RL reward-hack environments

claims.claim: Reasoning models' CoTs often fail to verbalize hints they use, including misalignment-related hints.
claims.evidence_quote: The overall faithfulness scores for both reasoning models remain low (25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1) (Figure 1).

claims.claim: Outcome-based RL improves faithfulness early but plateaus at moderate levels.
claims.evidence_quote: Outcome-based RL initially increases CoT faithfulness substantially but plateaus at an average of 28% on MMLU and 20% on GPQA.

claims.claim: Behaviors that can be done within a single forward pass (e.g. intention faking) are unlikely to be verbalized, so CoT monitoring cannot rule them out.
claims.evidence_quote: Moreover, intention faking does not seem like a reasoning-intensive task and can likely be done within single forward passes, making it unlikely to be faithfully verbalized in the CoT based on our experimental results.

numbers.what: Faithfulness on misalignment hints (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1)
numbers.quote: Particularly concerning are the low faithfulness scores on misalignment hints (20% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 29% for DeepSeek R1), which suggest that CoTs may hide problematic reasoning processes.

numbers.what: Relative faithfulness drop GPQA vs MMLU
numbers.quote: CoTs on GPQA are consistently less faithful than those on MMLU, by 44% relative for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 32% relative for DeepSeek R1.

numbers.what: Reward-hack exploitation vs verbalization in synthetic RL
numbers.quote: The model fully learns the reward hacks (reward > 0.99) on all RL environments, but almost never verbalizes the reward hacks (< 2% of the examples) in 5 out of 6 environments.

limitations: Multiple-choice settings with easily exploitable hints where CoT is not necessary; one kind of unintended behavior; faithfulness score is an upper bound on true faithfulness.
survey_notes: SECTION: safety (Sec. 14, CoT monitorability intro and latent-monitor paragraph). Statement 1: even for non-looped models the visible CoT is an imperfect window: "The overall faithfulness scores for both reasoning models remain low (25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1)", and reward hacks learned in RL are verbalized in "< 2% of the examples" in 5 of 6 environments. Statement 2: unfaithfulness is concentrated on behaviors that "can likely be done within single forward passes"; looping enlarges per-token serial computation, so the survey can argue (as an inference, not a result of this paper) that looping widens exactly the class of behavior that this paper shows CoT monitoring misses. CORRECTION/NUANCE for Sec. 14 opening ('Chain-of-thought reasoning gives overseers something to read'): add that the non-looped baseline is already low-faithfulness, so a looped-vs-standard monitorability comparison (2610.02741) measures a relative change against an imperfect baseline. Also relevant to open problem P6 (optimization pressure): outcome RL plateaus at 28% MMLU / 20% GPQA faithfulness even without training against a monitor.

title: Ulterior Motives: Detecting Misaligned Reasoning in Continuous Thought Models
relevance_reason: Latent-reasoning safety study on a Coconut-style (sequence-axis) continuous thought model; Huginn is named but explicitly not evaluated.
one_sentence: Builds MoralChain (12,000 scenarios) and a dual-trigger backdoored Coconut GPT-2 that reasons misaligned in latent thoughts while outputting aligned answers, and shows linear probes on early latent tokens detect this armed state.
key_contributions: Dual-trigger backdoor ([T] arms misaligned latent reasoning, [O] releases harmful output) that gives behavioral ground truth for misaligned latent states without decoding them.
MoralChain benchmark from Moral Stories with parallel 5-step moral and immoral reasoning paths.
Linear probes trained on [T][O] vs [O] transfer to the behaviorally identical [T] vs baseline pair, best at the first latent token (89.4%) and near chance at the sixth (58.3%).

setup.train_tokens_or_data: MoralChain: 10,000 train / 1,000 val / 1,000 test scenarios; Coconut curriculum, K = 5 stages, 5 epochs per stage
setup.loops_train: c = 2 latent tokens per reasoning step (sequence-axis continuous thoughts)
setup.baselines: baseline / control conditions of the same model

claims.claim: A continuous thought model can carry an armed misaligned latent state while producing moral outputs, and harmful output appears only when the release trigger is added.
claims.evidence_quote: We observe that baseline, armed ([T]), and control ([O]) all produce moral outputs >91% of the time (94.2%, 91.7%, and 93.8%, respectively), confirming that [T] alone does not leak misaligned reasoning into outputs and [O] alone has no effect.

claims.claim: Linear probes detect armed-but-benign latent states, most accurately at the earliest latent token, degrading toward chance at later tokens.
claims.evidence_quote: Transfer accuracy peaks at z1 (89.4%) and degrades monotonically to near-chance at z6 (58.3%), confirming that probes detect armed latent states, not outputs.

claims.claim: Results are limited to Coconut-style continuous thoughts; depth-recurrent Huginn and CODI are not evaluated.
claims.evidence_quote: We evaluate only Coconut-style continuous thought models—other architectures like CODI and Huginn may exhibit different latent dynamics.

numbers.what: Release condition ([T][O]) immoral output rate
numbers.quote: For release ([T][O]), moral actions drop to 12.4% and immoral actions rise to 87.6%.

numbers.what: Probe transfer AUROC at z1 to z6 ([T] vs baseline)
Base model size and compute
numbers.quote: We use GPT-2 (124M parameters) as our base model (Radford et al., 2019) and train for 5 epochs per stage across K = 5 stages with pmix = 0.3 and c = 2 latent tokens per reasoning step.

limitations: GPT-2 124M only; misalignment is implanted by backdoor training, not naturally emerging; social-reasoning domain only; Coconut-style models only (not CODI or Huginn); detection only, no intervention.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: SECTION: safety (Sec. 14, 'Reading latent computation directly' and Table tab:safety_map adjacent-evidence column) and neighbors (sequence-axis latent reasoning). Statement 1: in a sequence-axis continuous-thought model (GPT-2 124M), misaligned latent reasoning can coexist with aligned outputs: armed condition still gives moral outputs 91.7% of the time, while adding the release trigger gives 87.6% immoral outputs. Statement 2: a linear probe detects the armed state best at the first latent thought: "Transfer accuracy peaks at z1 (89.4%) and degrades monotonically to near-chance at z6 (58.3%)". Survey use: this is the closest existing positive result for a misbehavior monitor on latent reasoning; it is NOT a looped model. CORRECTION/NUANCE: (a) the paper groups Huginn with Coconut as models that 'feed continuous hidden states back as inputs'; the survey should not repeat this, since Huginn recurs in depth, and the paper itself says it evaluates "only Coconut-style continuous thought models". (b) Survey sentence 'No study builds a latent monitor for misbehavior such as deception or reward hacking on a looped model' remains true, but should cite this paper as the adjacent (sequence-axis, 124M, implanted backdoor) precedent and add it to the adjacent column of tab:safety_map. Open question for looped models: whether misalignment is similarly readable from early loop iterations (analogue of early latent tokens).

title: A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers
relevance_reason: Theory of length generalization for fixed-depth causal Transformers with APE/NoPE; no looping, but it explains which tasks need depth that grows with length.
one_sentence: Proves that, under an idealized norm-regularized inference procedure, causal Transformers with APE/NoPE length-generalize on functions expressible by a Limit Transformer (e.g. C-RASP programs), and shows copying, addition and PARITY fall outside; experiments match the predictions.
key_contributions: Limit Transformer formalism and Theorem 7: norm-regularized fitting on growing lengths ultimately length-generalizes for functions expressible by a single Limit Transformer with PERIODIC and LOCAL positional use.

C-RASP[periodic, local] programs translate to Limit Transformers (lower bound); communication-complexity upper bound shows copying arbitrary strings and n-digit addition are inexpressible; PARITY is not in C-RASP[periodic, local].
Experiments on 8 algorithmic tasks and 17 regular languages: length generalization succeeds where a C-RASP program exists and fails otherwise.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: algorithmic tasks and formal languages, training lengths up to 50, test lengths [51,100] and [101,150]
setup.baselines: C-RASP expressiveness vs circuit complexity and regular-language complexity as predictors
setup.benchmarks: 8 algorithmic problems (Zhou et al. 2024a style) and 17 regular languages (Bhattamishra et al. 2020)

claims.claim: Copying arbitrary strings and n-digit addition are not expressible by Limit Transformers, so any idealized solution sequence must grow depth, heads, norms, MLP size or precision with input length.
claims.evidence_quote: As a consequence, any run of the Inference Procedure on these functions will output solutions T1 , T2 , T3 , . . . for which the depth, number of heads, parameter norms or ranks, MLP dimensions, or precision p, must increase with the input length n

claims.claim: C-RASP expressiveness predicts empirical length generalization on regular languages: success exactly where a C-RASP[periodic, local] program was found.
claims.evidence_quote: We found C-RASP[periodic,local] programs for 13 of the languages and proved nonexistence for the others (Appendix E.1.2). Length generalization succeeded in those cases where we had found a C-RASP[periodic,local] program (see Figure 1 right).

claims.claim: The length-generalizable class (C-RASP[periodic, local]) is a proper subclass of TC0, suggesting a separation between TC0 and what fixed-depth APE Transformers length-generalize on.
claims.evidence_quote: All problems considered in Section 5 are in TC0 , but empirical length generalization behavior largely tracks C-RASP[periodic,local] expressiveness, which defines a proper subclass of TC0 (Appendix C.3.1).

numbers.what: Regular languages with a C-RASP[periodic,local] program out of 17
numbers.quote: We found C-RASP[periodic,local] programs for 13 of the languages and proved nonexistence for the others (Appendix E.1.2).

limitations: Idealized asymptotic identification of a global minimum with perfect knowledge of the training distribution; no SGD dynamics; no practical bound on the threshold length; APE/NoPE only.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
survey_notes: SECTION: theory (Sec. 9, length generalization subsection) as the non-looped baseline. Statement 1: for fixed-depth causal Transformers, copying arbitrary strings and n-digit addition are provably not length-generalizable under the idealized procedure, because any fitted solution sequence must have "depth, number of heads, parameter norms or ranks, MLP dimensions, or precision p, must increase with the input length n". This is the theoretical reason the looped-extrapolation literature uses addition and parity as test beds: looping is a way to grow depth with n at constant parameters (survey inference; this paper does not study loops). Statement 2: PARITY is not in C-RASP[periodic, local], and empirical success on 17 regular languages tracks C-RASP (13 expressible, generalization succeeded where a program exists). Survey should cite this when contrasting fixed-depth failure on parity/addition with looped models that couple loop count to length (2409.15647, 2202.05826). CAVEAT for the survey: the framework's regularizer bounds depth, so looped models with input-dependent loop counts fall outside it; no claim that looping provably fixes these tasks follows from this paper. No correction to existing survey text; it is a missing anchor citation for Sec. 9.4.

title: Lower Bounds for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Hard-Attention Transformers
relevance_reason: CoT-length lower bounds for fixed-depth (bounded layers and heads) UHAT Transformers; the cost baseline that depth growth (looping) is meant to avoid.
one_sentence: Proves in the unique-hard-attention model that CoTs for high-sensitivity problems (PARITY, multiplication, median, DAG reachability) must have at least linear length, tight up to log factors, and that dot-by-dot filler CoTs for PARITY need superpolynomial length.
key_contributions: Generic CoT bound (Theorem 3.3) via a depth-reduction (restriction) argument for UHAT Transformers with uniformly bounded layers and heads.
Omega(N) CoT lower bounds for PARITY and multiplication, Omega(|E| log |V|) for a TC0 family of DAG reachability, with matching constructions up to log factors.
Superpolynomial separation between full CoT (Theta(N)) and dot-by-dot CoT for PARITY; small-Transformer experiments on multiplication and reachability.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: binary multiplication up to 16 digits; random DAGs with 5 to 35 vertices

claims.claim: Any UHAT chain of thought for PARITY needs length linear in the input.
claims.evidence_quote: In this model, we rigorously prove that the CoT for PARITY described above is optimal up to constant factors (Theorem 4.2).

claims.claim: Across PARITY, multiplication, median and reachability, CoT length must scale at least linearly, and the bounds are tight up to logarithmic factors.
claims.evidence_quote: Across tasks, we show that CoT lengths need to scale at least linearly in the size of the original problem. We further show that our bounds are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

claims.claim: Filler-token (dot-by-dot) CoTs face an even stronger barrier: for PARITY their length cannot be polynomially bounded; the authors suggest logarithmic depth growth as a way around these limits.
claims.evidence_quote: Logarithmic growth of the depth may be one way to overcome these (Merrill & Sabharwal, 2024b); within fixed-depth architectures, certain SSM architectures overcome at least the difficulty of PARITY (Grazzi et al., 2024).

numbers.what: Multiplication experiment: model size and digits
numbers.quote: We trained small transformers (2 layers, 2 heads) to multiply binary numbers with up to 16 digits, either directly, or with the O(N log N ) CoT from Theorem 4.6.

numbers.what: DAG reachability CoT lower bound
numbers.quote: There is a family G of DAGs inside which reachability is solvable in T C 0 , but cannot be represented by a transformer at sublinear average sensitivity. A UHAT CoT needs length Ω (|E| log |V |).

limitations: Unique hard attention abstraction (bounds transfer to fixed-precision softmax via an upper bound); finite input alphabet; bounded layers and heads; experiments small-scale.
venue: Proceedings of the 42 nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025
survey_notes: SECTION: theory (Sec. 9.2, looped models versus chain of thought; add a row or sentence to tab:loop_vs_cot as the fixed-depth cost baseline); secondary: safety (filler tokens). Statement 1: for fixed-depth Transformers the token cost of CoT on high-sensitivity tasks is provably linear: "Across tasks, we show that CoT lengths need to scale at least linearly in the size of the original problem" (PARITY, multiplication, median, reachability), tight up to log factors. Statement 2: the authors name depth growth as the escape route: "Logarithmic growth of the depth may be one way to overcome these", which is exactly what looped models with input-dependent loop counts supply (link to 2502.17416, 2503.03961, 2505.18948 already in Sec. 9). Also: filler-token CoT for PARITY must be superpolynomially long, i.e. invisible computation via filler tokens is severely limited at fixed depth; looping removes this fixed-depth barrier, which strengthens the Sec. 14 argument that looping is the architectural change most likely to move high-sensitivity computation out of the visible trace (survey inference). No correction to existing survey text.

title: Perfect diffusion is $\mathsf{TC}^0$ -- Bad diffusion is Turing-complete
relevance_reason: Complexity theory of iterative refinement in diffusion LMs (refinement-axis recurrence), not depth looping; argues convergence of iteration caps serial computation.
one_sentence: Proves that diffusion models whose score network is TC0 and exactly matches a score function can only do TC0 language modeling because denoising converges in a number of steps independent of input length, while unconstrained 'bad' score fields are Turing-complete.
key_contributions: Main theorem: exact score matching plus a TC0 score network implies TC0, since the required diffusion time T does not grow with input length n.
A 'pinball machine' construction showing that a non-convergent smooth force field can simulate any counter machine (Turing-complete).

Conjectures for good-but-imperfect and discrete diffusion, testable predictions (performance cliffs with fixed denoising steps), and a call for architectures that interpolate sequential and parallel computation.

claims.claim: Perfect score-matching diffusion is limited to TC0 because its convergence is fast and does not scale with input length.
claims.evidence_quote: In one direction, a network that exactly computes the score function of some initial distribution can only perform language modeling within the TC0 complexity class, reflecting limitations tied to rapid convergence.

claims.claim: Without any score-matching requirement, diffusion dynamics can simulate any Turing machine via a non-convergent force field.
claims.evidence_quote: By constructing a “bad” diffusion model with a specifically designed, non-convergent score function, we showed that such systems can achieve Turing-completeness, capable of simulating arbitrary sequential computation via a pinball machine analogy.

claims.claim: Predicted empirical signature: more denoising steps beyond a threshold help little on TC0 tasks but keep helping on tasks outside TC0; the author proposes architectures that switch between sequential and parallel modes.
claims.evidence_quote: Adding more denoising steps beyond a certain threshold should yield minimal improvements for TC0 tasks but continued improvements for tasks outside this complexity class.

limitations: Results only for the two extremes (exact score vs. no constraint); the realistic approximate case is conjectured, not proved; continuous-space SMLD formulation; no experiments.
builds_on: Li et al. 2024 (2402.12875, CoT serial problems)
survey_notes: SECTION: neighbors (Sec. 13, diffusion language models) and theory (Sec. 9, loop count as circuit depth). Statement 1: iterating a network does not by itself add serial computation if the iteration converges in input-independent time: exact score-matching diffusion "can only perform language modeling within the TC0 complexity class, reflecting limitations tied to rapid convergence". This sharpens the survey's contrast between refinement recurrence (diffusion) and depth recurrence: looped models gain expressivity only when the loop count grows with input (Sec. 9 results), not from iteration per se. Statement 2: the paper predicts that extra denoising steps "should yield minimal improvements for TC0 tasks", which is consistent with the Sec. 12 finding that loop depth beats extra denoising steps at matched FLOPs (2609.40305), and it explicitly calls for architectures that "interpolate between sequential and parallel modes", a description that fits adaptive-depth looped models (survey framing, not the paper's). TENSION to flag: survey Sec. 13 cites 2510.03206 that continuous diffusion is more expressive than discrete diffusion and looped Transformers; this paper bounds exact-score continuous diffusion by TC0 and conjectures discrete diffusion is TC0 regardless of score quality, so the expressivity ranking depends on whether the score is exact. Also parallels the DEQ caution in Sec. 13 (converged iteration cannot keep adding computation) and is in tension with fixed-point/settling objectives (2608.18222) only superficially: those concern stability of extrapolation, not expressive power.

title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
relevance_reason: Foundational CoT expressivity result for constant-depth Transformers; the sequence-axis baseline against which looped (depth-axis) expressivity is compared.
one_sentence: Shows constant-depth, constant-precision Transformers without CoT lie in AC0, that T CoT steps let them simulate any size-T boolean circuit, and that CoT sharply helps low-depth models on inherently serial tasks (S5 composition, iterated squaring, circuit value).
key_contributions: Tighter upper bound: constant-depth Transformers with constant-bit precision express only AC0 (TC0 with log precision); O(log n) CoT steps do not go beyond AC0.

With T CoT steps and O(log n) embedding size, constant-depth constant-precision Transformers compute any function computed by a size-T circuit; polynomial CoT gives P/poly; linear CoT gives all regular languages including the NC1-complete S5 word problem.
Experiments on modular addition, permutation composition, iterated squaring and circuit value problem: CoT beats hint and base training, especially at small depth.

setup.model_sizes: small decoder-only Transformers of varying depth
setup.train_tokens_or_data: online synthetic data per task and sequence length
setup.baselines: base (no CoT) and hint (CoT as auxiliary labels) training
setup.benchmarks: modular addition (C7, C2), permutation composition (S5), iterated squaring, circuit value problem

claims.claim: Without CoT, the serial computation of a Transformer is bounded by its depth; with T intermediate steps it grows to T, which can scale with input length while depth stays fixed.
claims.evidence_quote: Intuitively, without CoT, the number of serial computations conducted by the transformer is bounded by the depth (which is considered as a fixed constant for this work), whereas with T intermediate steps, the number of serial computations possible is boosted to T .

claims.claim: Constant-depth constant-precision Transformers without CoT are in AC0, but T CoT steps suffice to compute any size-T circuit.
claims.evidence_quote: However, with T steps of CoT, constant-depth transformers using constant-bit precision and O(log n) embedding size can solve any problem solvable by boolean circuits of size T .

claims.claim: Logarithmically many CoT steps add no power beyond AC0.
claims.evidence_quote: Interestingly, we also show that logarithmically many CoT steps do not allow the transformer to compute functions beyond AC0 . (Theorem 3.1)

claims.claim: Empirically, CoT drastically improves low-depth Transformers on inherently serial tasks; without CoT, S5 composition accuracy stays near chance.
claims.evidence_quote: Note for the most time the accuracy without CoT is ∼ 20%, which is no better than randomly guessing a number between 1 and 5.

numbers.what: Accuracy without CoT on S5 permutation composition
numbers.quote: Note for the most time the accuracy without CoT is ∼ 20%, which is no better than randomly guessing a number between 1 and 5.

limitations: Expressiveness only (not learnability beyond synthetic tasks); constant depth assumed; CoT metric in experiments is teacher-forced token accuracy (a lower bound).
builds_on: Looped transformers as programmable computers (2301.13196, cited)
survey_notes: SECTION: theory (Sec. 9.2, looped models versus chain of thought; tab:loop_vs_cot). Statement 1: the sequence-axis baseline: "with T steps of CoT, constant-depth transformers using constant-bit precision and O(log n) embedding size can solve any problem solvable by boolean circuits of size T", i.e. CoT steps buy circuit SIZE. This is the origin of the size-vs-depth framing the survey attributes to 2509.25239 (CoT steps = circuit size; loop iterations = circuit depth); cite both. Statement 2: "logarithmically many CoT steps do not allow the transformer to compute functions beyond AC0" (constant precision), whereas O(log n) loops with padding reach NC1/TC1-type classes (2505.18948, 2605.30523 in survey); this gives the cleanest small-budget separation in favor of loops. Precision dependence (AC0 at constant precision, TC0 at log precision) matches the survey sentence that precision decides between AC and TC classes (2605.30523). Note: the depth-is-fixed premise, "without CoT, the number of serial computations conducted by the transformer is bounded by the depth", is exactly what looping relaxes. No correction; add as a citation in Sec. 9.2 and the CoT row of tab:axes (Sec. 3).

title: Continuous Chain of Thought Enables Parallel Exploration and Reasoning
relevance_reason: Sequence-axis continuous CoT (Coconut lineage) with theory of superposed parallel traces; not depth looping, but the closest mechanistic neighbor for latent-state search.
one_sentence: Proposes CoT2, continuous tokens formed as superpositions of vocabulary embeddings, with budget-constrained distribution supervision and multi-token sampling for GRPO; shows it tracks multiple search traces in parallel, limited by embedding dimension, on MNNS, ProntoQA and ProsQA.
key_contributions: Continuous supervision (CSFT) that fits outputs to the empirical token distribution of B teacher traces, interpolating from discrete CoT (B = 1) to full search.

Theory: one-layer Transformer solves Minimum Non-Negative Sum with CoT2; multi-token sampling with budget K is as expressive as self-consistency over K traces; information-packing bound d = Omega(B log(v/B)).
Policy optimization for continuous tokens (multi-token sampling, Dirichlet sampling) that improves over SFT/CSFT.

setup.model_sizes: GPT2 with 1 layer 1 head, 2 layers 2 heads, 4 layers 4 heads; d in {16, 24, 32, 40}

claims.claim: Continuous tokens let the model keep multiple reasoning traces in superposition and defer commitment, outperforming COCONUT, discrete CoT and no-CoT on search tasks; discrete CoT needs multiple samples to match single-shot CoT2.
claims.evidence_quote: (a): Discrete CoT model requires multiple samplings (Pass@k) to match the single-shot performance of CoT2 model on MNNS (10-run avgs). (b): CoT2 model outperforms COCONUT, discrete CoT, and no-CoT in tasks involving search, like MNNS and ProsQA (5-run avgs).

claims.claim: Parallelism is capped by embedding capacity: superposing more traces helps only when the embedding dimension is large enough.
claims.evidence_quote: This indicates a capacity–parallelism tradeoff in which larger B helps only when d is sufficiently large to represent the superposed traces.

claims.claim: The authors position CoT2 alongside looped Transformers as reasoning with continuous representations.
claims.evidence_quote: Another line of work has found looped transformers to be effective on reasoning problems [Giannou et al., 2023, Geiping et al., 2025], notably being able to mimic CoT [Saunshi et al., 2025] with a sufficient number of iterations.

numbers.what: Information-packing bound on embedding dimension for budget-B superposition over v states
numbers.quote: showing that robust decoding of a budget-B superposition over v candidate states requires embedding d = Ω B log(v/B) in the worst case.

numbers.what: SFT accuracies before GRPO on MNNS (1-layer 1-head GPT2, d = 24 and 32)
numbers.quote: We use 4 input digits in 1-9 with 1-layer, 1-head GPT2 at embedding dimensions d = 24 and d = 32, with SFT accuracies of 39.76% and 43.50%, respectively.

limitations: Small GPT2 models on synthetic search tasks; full-budget supervision requires access to a search algorithm's traces.
survey_notes: SECTION: neighbors (Sec. 13, sequence-axis latent reasoning); secondary: mechanisms (latent search) and safety. Statement 1: continuous thoughts can hold several search branches at once and defer the decision: "CoT2 model outperforms COCONUT, discrete CoT, and no-CoT in tasks involving search, like MNNS and ProsQA", and discrete CoT needs Pass@k to match single-shot CoT2. Statement 2: the parallelism is bounded by width, not steps: "larger B helps only when d is sufficiently large to represent the superposed traces", with a worst-case requirement d = Omega(B log(v/B)). Survey use: gives a width-based capacity argument that should transfer to looped hidden states (each loop iteration also carries a d-dimensional continuous state), suggesting looped models' latent search capacity is set by hidden width; this is a hypothesis for the survey to state, not a tested result. All results at <= 4-layer GPT2 on synthetic tasks. Safety angle: superposed latent traces are exactly the kind of state that the opaque-serial-depth framework (2603.09786) treats as non-interpretable. No correction to existing survey text.

title: Quantization Robustness of Monotone Operator Equilibrium Networks
relevance_reason: Quantization theory for a single-layer implicit (fixed-point) network on MNIST; equilibrium limit of weight-tied looping, not a looped LM.
one_sentence: Treats weight quantization of a monotone operator equilibrium network as a spectral perturbation and proves that if the perturbation norm is below the monotonicity margin the quantized fixed-point solver still converges with a bounded equilibrium shift; MNIST experiments show the predicted divergence threshold.
key_contributions: Certificate ||Delta W||_2 < m (monotonicity margin) under which the quantized MonDEQ keeps existence, uniqueness, linear convergence and a bounded equilibrium displacement; the same threshold certifies the backward solve.
Displacement bound and a condition number linking bit-width to forward error.
MNIST validation: 3- and 4-bit post-training quantization diverge, 5-bit and above converge; quantization-aware training recovers convergence at 4 bits.

setup.model_sizes: single-layer MonDEQ with n = 100 hidden units
setup.loops_train: forward-backward splitting to relative residual 1e-5 or 2000 iterations
setup.loops_test: same solver; about 1730 iterations at 5-bit and 450 at 8-bit

claims.claim: Convergence of the quantized solver is guaranteed whenever the spectral-norm weight perturbation is smaller than the monotonicity margin, and the equilibrium shift is bounded.
claims.evidence_quote: We provide an explicit quantizationpreservation certificate: a single computable check on the weight perturbation determines whether the quantized network retains existence, uniqueness, linear convergence, and a bounded displacement of its equilibrium.

claims.claim: Empirically the divergence threshold matches the predicted ratio of perturbation to margin: 3- and 4-bit PTQ diverge, 5-bit and above converge.
claims.evidence_quote: The non-convergence/convergence transition aligns with ∥∆W ∥2 /m = 1: 3-bit (ratio 5.36) and 4-bit (2.66) diverge, 5-bit and above converge.

claims.claim: Quantization-aware training, made well defined by the backward-pass guarantee, recovers convergence at 4 bits where PTQ fails.
claims.evidence_quote: Quantization-aware training recovers convergence at 4 bits where post-training quantization fails, enabled by the backward-pass guarantee of Theorem 5.

numbers.what: 8-bit vs 32-bit accuracy and storage
numbers.quote: At 8 bits, weight storage drops 4× versus 32-bit floating-point with 98.24% vs. 98.22% accuracy.

numbers.what: QAT at 4 bits accuracy and margin
numbers.quote: QAT learns weights with m e = 0.006 > 0, achieving 96.78% accuracy at a smaller margin (m = 0.184 vs. 0.227).

numbers.what: Full-precision model accuracy and margin
numbers.quote: The trained model achieves 98.22% test accuracy with m = 0.227, L = 1.845, κ = L/m = 8.13.

limitations: Uniform symmetric per-tensor quantization of a single-layer MonDEQ on MNIST only; condition is sufficient but not necessary (5-bit converges despite violating it); multi-layer and per-channel schemes left open.
venue: This is the authors' accepted version; the version of record will appear in IEEE Control Systems Letters via its DOI.
survey_notes: SECTION: systems (Sec. 8.4, quantization and numerics); secondary: neighbors (DEQ paragraph). Statement 1: for a provably contractive (monotone) fixed-point network, quantization error acts as a bounded shift of the equilibrium as long as ||Delta W||_2 < m; beyond that threshold the iteration diverges: "3-bit (ratio 5.36) and 4-bit (2.66) diverge, 5-bit and above converge". This is a formal, small-scale version of the 'settling loops only shift their fixed point' argument in 2609.39277 and supports that side of the disagreement the survey describes (error accumulation vs fixed-point shift): accumulation is the failure mode only once the margin is destroyed. Statement 2: the practical pattern matches the looped-LM literature: "At 8 bits, weight storage drops 4× versus 32-bit floating-point with 98.24% vs. 98.22% accuracy", per-tensor 4-bit PTQ fails, and QAT recovers 4 bits (96.78%). Survey can say the 8-bit-safe / 4-bit-needs-care rule also holds for equilibrium models with a certificate. CAVEAT: single-layer MonDEQ on MNIST, per-tensor quantization, no LM; looped LMs lack a monotonicity margin (Huginn does not settle per 2608.18222), so the certificate does not transfer directly. No correction; supporting citation for Sec. 8.4.

title: Fractal basins trap latent reasoning
relevance_reason: Dynamical-systems analysis of weight-tied recurrent-depth reasoners (EqR, FPRM, TRM, Parcae-140M, a looped Transformer) iterated in depth; all probed models loop a shared block.
one_sentence: Varying only the initial latent state of released recurrent-depth reasoners, finds that convergence-time basins become fractal on hard Sudoku, maze, Countdown and ARC instances, caused by transient chaos from saddle points that decode to nearly-correct solutions and that appear as a training bifurcation.
key_contributions: Basin-map probe: hold model and puzzle fixed, vary the initial latent state on a random 2D slice, and record loops until the decoded output stops changing; basin entropy rises with mean loops to converge across four architectures and tasks.

Mechanism: slow trajectories are scattered by weakly-unstable saddle points that decode to nearly-correct solutions (dead ends in mazes, repeated digits in Sudoku); fast Lyapunov indicator tracks how often the decoded answer switches.

In a small looped Transformer trained on integer linear systems over F_3, solvability, basin entropy and unstable saddle directions appear together at a bifurcation about 150k steps into training; only multi-step (core) variables show positive FTLE.

setup.model_sizes: released checkpoints of Equilibrium Reasoners, Fixed-Point Reasoning Models, Tiny Recursive Model; Parcae 140M looped LM finetuned on Countdown; encoder-only looped Transformer on F_3 linear systems
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Unique / Maze-Hard, Countdown, ARC-AGI-1; integer linear systems p = 3, M = N = 8
setup.loops_test: EqR fixed 24 iterations; FPRM residual threshold with caps of 1000 (Sudoku) and 100 (mazes) iterations
setup.benchmarks: basin entropy, fast Lyapunov indicator, finite-time Lyapunov exponents, settling time

claims.claim: On hard instances, convergence time of recurrent reasoners is a fractal function of the initial latent state, so tiny initialization changes can change loops-to-converge by orders of magnitude.
claims.evidence_quote: Across diverse reasoning models, we observe complex basins of attraction when we label initial conditions by their convergence time, and we find that these basins become self-similar fractals on harder tasks, like Sudoku puzzles (Fig. 1B).

claims.claim: Basin entropy strongly correlates with the mean number of loops needed to converge, a proxy for task difficulty.
claims.evidence_quote: We find that the basin entropy strongly correlates with the number of iterations, a measure of overall task difficulty. These findings persist across alternative architectures (Appendix C) and basin complexity metrics (Appendix D).

claims.claim: Slow-converging trajectories are trapped near saddle points that decode to nearly-correct solutions.
claims.evidence_quote: Decoding these meandering trajectories into problem states reveals that reasoning becomes trapped near answers that are nearly, but not quite, correct. In mazes, saddle regions correspond to dead ends; in Sudoku puzzles, they represent grids with repeated digits (Fig. 3D).

claims.claim: Fractal basins appear at a training bifurcation when the looped model acquires multi-step reasoning; incorrect fixed points become saddles.
claims.evidence_quote: We thus find that the bifurcation to solvability during training occurs when the model gains multi-step reasoning capability. This, in turn, allows the model to escape from incorrect solutions in the core, but it leads to transient chaos and fractal basins.

numbers.what: Training step of the solvability bifurcation in the looped linear-system solver
numbers.quote: Panels correspond to a series of training steps around the bifurcation that occurs 150k steps into training, when accurate solving first emerges.

numbers.what: Size of the looped LM probed
numbers.quote: Parcae [3] is a 140M parameter looped language model that we finetuned on the Countdown arithmetic task.

limitations: Probes only recurrent-depth/equilibrium models with extractable per-loop latents (largest 140M); abstract's claims about 'reasoning models' generally are not tested on chain-of-thought LLMs; EqR noise disabled and loop budgets fixed for the probe; correlational evidence from 2D slices of the initial-state space.
survey_notes: SECTION: mechanisms (Sec. 10, latent dynamics); secondary: adaptive depth (Sec. 5, convergence-based halting) and capabilities (Sec. 11.2, recursive reasoners). Statement 1: on hard puzzles, the number of loops a recurrent reasoner needs is a fractal function of its initial latent state: "these basins become self-similar fractals on harder tasks", and "the basin entropy strongly correlates with the number of iterations, a measure of overall task difficulty" (EqR, FPRM, TRM, Parcae-140M). Statement 2: extra loops on hard instances are spent near saddles that decode to near-solutions: "reasoning becomes trapped near answers that are nearly, but not quite, correct"; this gives a mechanism for the survey's observation that test-time recursion helps on Sudoku but plateaus elsewhere. Implications for the survey: (a) Sec. 5 convergence-based halting: settling time on hard inputs is extremely sensitive to the (often random) initial state used by Huginn-style and HRM/TRM-style models, so per-input loop budgets are inherently noisy; (b) Sec. 10: complements 'Huginn does not settle' (2608.18222): here models DO converge, but via transient chaos. NUANCE/CORRECTION: the abstract says 'diverse leading reasoning models' and 'reasoning traces', but every probed model is a recurrent-depth/equilibrium model of at most 140M; the survey must not cite it as evidence about chain-of-thought LLMs. No numbers on accuracy or compute; analysis only.

title: Neural Cellular Automata for ARC-AGI
relevance_reason: Weight-tied local update rule iterated in time (NCA) trained per ARC task; recurrent computation without attention, classified adjacent for consistency with 2609.36126.
one_sentence: Trains a ~10k-parameter neural cellular automaton from scratch per ARC-AGI-1 task with BPTT and loss at every step; it perfectly solves 23 of 172 feasible training tasks (13.37%) and shows size generalization on some tasks.
key_contributions: NCA adapted to ARC: one-hot color channels plus 20 hidden channels, learnable convolution instead of Sobel filters, layernorm, full-state replacement s_{t+1} = f(s_t), 10 steps.
Training recipe: loss at every step (not only final), and randomized asynchronous update-mask probability so the model also runs synchronously at test time.
Analysis of successes (e.g. spiral rule scales to 100x100 grids) and failures (overfitting to training examples, color generalization impossible by design).

setup.model_sizes: just over 10,000 parameters per task (some tasks under 2500)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: per-task training on ARC-AGI-1 public training examples, 800 epochs, no pretraining
setup.loops_train: 10 time steps, stochastic update mask probability in [0, 0.75]
setup.loops_test: 10 steps; spiral task run longer on 100x100 grids
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1 public training set (400 tasks; 172 feasible)

claims.claim: Per-task NCAs with no pretraining solve a modest fraction of feasible ARC tasks perfectly.
claims.evidence_quote: Thus, there were 172 feasible tasks. Of these, the NCA approach solved 23 perfectly, resulting in a success rate of 13.37%.

claims.claim: Supervising every step rather than only the final step was needed for stability and generalization, because errors compound across iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: Small errors tend to compound over time; constant supervision mitigates this problem.

claims.claim: Learned local iterative rules can generalize in size: a spiral rule trained on small grids runs coherently on 100x100 grids by using more steps.
claims.evidence_quote: The system learned a compact, iterative rule that is precise enough to have an effective degree of size invariance, capable of scaling up to a 100×100 grid (Figure 3).

numbers.what: Model size
numbers.quote: They have just over 10,000 parameters. In practice, much fewer than 20 hidden channels were needed for a majority of tasks, allowing models smaller than 2500 parameters to perform similarly in some cases.

numbers.what: Task scoping
numbers.value: 138 out of scope (grid size), 90 with unseen colors, 172 feasible
numbers.quote: Of the 400 public training tasks, 138 were out of scope because of the input-output grid size restriction.

limitations: Fixed input-output grid size; cannot generalize to unseen colors; evaluated on the public training set, not the evaluation set; same hyperparameters for all tasks; per-step supervision makes convergence greedy.
survey_notes: SECTION: beyond language (Sec. 12) and capabilities (Sec. 11.2, ARC/puzzle reasoners) as an attention-free weight-tied iterative baseline. Statement 1: a per-task NCA of about 10k parameters with no pretraining solves 23 of 172 feasible ARC-AGI-1 training tasks: "the NCA approach solved 23 perfectly, resulting in a success rate of 13.37%" (public training set, not the eval set; not comparable to TRM/HRM numbers). Statement 2: the training lesson matches the recursive-reasoning literature: per-step supervision was needed because "Small errors tend to compound over time; constant supervision mitigates this problem", and a learned local rule can extrapolate in size (spiral to 100x100) by running more steps. Survey use: early (2025) evidence that iterating a tiny shared rule is a viable inductive bias for ARC-style grids; the later 2609.36126 NCA reasoner reports much higher ARC numbers with RE-ARC pretraining. CAVEAT: classified adjacent (no attention, per-task models), consistent with how 2609.36126 was classified by recursive_reasoning_b. No correction to existing survey text.

title: State Representation and Termination for Recursive Reasoning Systems
relevance_reason: Theoretical termination criterion for agent/RAG/refinement loops over an explicit knowledge-graph state; mentions TRM but has no neural looped model and no experiments.
one_sentence: Proposes an epistemic state graph for iterative reasoning systems and an 'order-gap' stopping rule (distance between expand-then-consolidate and consolidate-then-expand), with a local non-degeneracy theorem at the fixed point and only a closed-form 2D illustration.
key_contributions: Epistemic state graph (claims, evidential relations, conflicts, partial answers, open questions, confidence) with a Euclidean embedding.

Order-gap termination: stop when the state is insensitive to the order of expansion and consolidation; Theorem 5.2 gives a necessary and sufficient local condition for the linearised criterion to be non-degenerate.
Sketches applications to recursive language models, TRM-style latent loops, agent loops, tree-of-thought, theorem proving and continual learning.

claims.claim: A small order-gap indicates that further iteration is unlikely to help; the main theorem says when this criterion is informative, as a local (not global) result.
claims.evidence_quote: Our main result gives a necessary and sufficient condition for the linearised order-gap to be non-degenerate near the fixed point, showing when the criterion is informative rather than algebraically vacuous. This is a local condition, not a global convergence guarantee.

claims.claim: Existing recursive systems including TRM leave state and termination implicit and do not derive termination from their operator structure.
claims.evidence_quote: The RLM's aggregate state is an unstructured REPL buffer; the TRM's is a latent vector. Neither derives its termination criterion from the operator structure.

limitations: No empirical evaluation (the illustration is expository); local result only; no connection to answer error; empirical comparison against fixed-budget and confidence-threshold baselines left to future work.
survey_notes: SECTION: adaptive depth (Sec. 5, loop-count policies; convergence criteria) at most as a one-line pointer. Statement 1: proposes a training-free termination signal based on operator non-commutativity, with a local guarantee only: "This is a local condition, not a global convergence guarantee." Statement 2: explicitly notes that TRM's state is "a latent vector" and that neither TRM nor RLM "derives its termination criterion from the operator structure"; the survey can use this to motivate that learned halting in recursive reasoners lacks a principled stopping signal. CAVEAT: no experiments, no neural looped model; it does not test the criterion on TRM. Recommendation: low priority; cite only if Sec. 5 discusses convergence-based halting alternatives. No correction to existing survey text.

title: DACT-BERT: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for an Efficient BERT Inference
relevance_reason: Differentiable ACT-style halting over BERT's unshared layers (early exit); halting-mechanism precursor, not a looped model.
one_sentence: Adds a differentiable adaptive-computation-time module (classifier plus sigmoid halting value after each block) to BERT/RoBERTa, trains end to end with a ponder penalty, and halts when the top class provably cannot change; beats DeeBERT and PABEE on GLUE at low compute.
key_contributions: Adapts DACT (a fully differentiable ACT variant originally for recurrent models) to Transformer blocks: accumulated answer interpolated by a monotone function of earlier confidences, loss plus tau times the sum of halting values.
Inference halts once upper and lower bounds show the top class cannot be overtaken by running more blocks.
Full differentiability lets the backbone be fine-tuned for reduced compute; compute saved is stable for a given ponder penalty, unlike DeeBERT's entropy threshold.

setup.loops_test: up to 12 blocks, halting per input
setup.baselines: DeeBERT, PABEE (same backbones), static backbones, DistilBERT

claims.claim: At limited compute, DACT-BERT outperforms early-exit baselines on almost every GLUE task.
claims.regime: iso_param (same backbones); compute measured as fraction of layers used
claims.evidence_quote: On the other hand, when using limited amounts of computation our model outperforms the alternatives in almost every task, especially in tasks for with more training data available.

claims.claim: Learned halting gives stable compute savings for a fixed ponder penalty, while entropy-threshold early exit is hyperparameter-sensitive.
claims.evidence_quote: As the same values of ponder penalties give rise to similar efficiency outputs. By contrast, DeeBERT proves to be highly sensitive to the chosen value for the entropy hyperparameter.

claims.claim: Halting is triggered when further blocks cannot change the predicted class, not by a confidence threshold.
claims.evidence_quote: That is, the model stops executing additional blocks once it finds that doing so will not change the class with maximum probability in the output because the difference between the top class and the rest is insurmountable.

limitations: Classification (GLUE) only; unshared layers so depth cannot exceed 12; results reported as curves without tabulated numbers; short paper.
survey_notes: SECTION: adaptive depth (Sec. 5, learned halting row of the loop-policy table) and neighbors (Sec. 13.3, adaptive depth without sharing). Statement 1: a differentiable ACT variant transfers to Transformer blocks and halts by a certificate, not a threshold: "the model stops executing additional blocks once it finds that doing so will not change the class with maximum probability". Statement 2: in this unshared, classification setting learned halting was stable: "the same values of ponder penalties give rise to similar efficiency outputs" whereas "DeeBERT proves to be highly sensitive to the chosen value for the entropy hyperparameter". NUANCE for survey Sec. 5 ('Learned halting is fragile'): DACT-BERT is a counterexample in a fine-tuned classifier with unshared layers; the fragility the survey reports (collapse to first iteration, 2610.00673) concerns jointly pretrained weight-tied LMs. The survey should scope the fragility claim to pretrained looped LMs rather than learned halting in general. No numbers in text (figure-only results).

title: Hyper-Connections
relevance_reason: Residual-connection replacement for standard (unshared) Transformers; component later used at loop level by Hyperloop (2604.21254), not itself looped.
one_sentence: Replaces residual connections with n parallel hidden streams joined by learnable (static or input-dependent) depth- and width-connections; in OLMo-1B/7B and OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining it lowers loss, speeds convergence and reduces adjacent-layer representation collapse at negligible extra cost.
key_contributions: Hyper-connections: expand the hidden state to n copies; learnable depth-connections generalize residual weights and width-connections mix the copies, letting the network reweight or rearrange layers sequentially or in parallel; Pre-Norm and Post-Norm are special non-trainable cases.
Dynamic hyper-connections (DHC) predict connection weights from the input; n = 1 does not help, n = 4 is best, n = 8 adds little.
Pretraining evidence on dense (1B, 7B) and MoE (OLMoE-1B-7B) LMs plus vision; lower similarity between adjacent-layer features and no loss spikes.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 500B tokens for 1B ablations and OLMoE; 7B evaluated after 400B+ tokens
setup.baselines: Pre-Norm residual baselines (OLMo, OLMoE); related methods incl. ResiDual
setup.benchmarks: C4-en and V2/V3 validation loss/PPL; HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge, SciQ and other downstream tasks; vision tasks

claims.claim: Dynamic hyper-connections make an MoE LM converge 1.8x faster and improve ARC-Challenge by 6 points at 500B tokens.
claims.regime: iso_data (same 500B tokens); near iso_param and iso_infer_flop (overhead negligible)
claims.evidence_quote: The model utilizing DHC converges 1.8 times faster and shows an improvement of 6 points on ARC-Challenge compared to the baseline trained with 500 B tokens.

claims.claim: Pre-Norm baselines show representation collapse (high adjacent-layer similarity); HC lowers that similarity, suggesting each layer contributes more.
claims.evidence_quote: According to our visualization analysis, as shown in Fig.3, the baseline model tends toward representation collapse, characterized by high similarity between features of adjacent layers.

claims.claim: Expansion rate matters: a single stream (n = 1) is worse than baseline; n > 1 helps, saturating at n = 4.
claims.evidence_quote: We observe that with an expansion rate of n = 1, the performance of DHC is inferior to the baseline. However, for n > 1, DHC significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving superior results at n = 4, with the increase to n = 8 providing minimal additional benefits.

numbers.what: OLMo-7B vs OLMo-7B-DHCx4 params, forward GFLOPs per token, V2 loss, V3 loss, task avg
OLMo-7B-DHCx4 improvement in V2 loss and PPL
numbers.quote: In the V2 evaluation, OLMo-7B-DHC×4 shows improvements of 0.022 for loss and 0.293 for PPL.

limitations: Not studied with weight sharing or looping; memory of n hidden streams per token not emphasized; gains at 7B are modest (0.9 points average).
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
survey_notes: SECTION: design space (Sec. 5.2, state passing between iterations; 'Access to earlier iterations helps consistently' and 'Plain chaining is not enough'). Statement 1: HC is the component behind Hyperloop's 'loop-level hyper-connections' (tab. in Sec. 5): it replaces the single residual stream by n streams with learnable depth/width mixing at almost no FLOP cost (OLMo-7B 13.36 vs 13.38 forward GFLOPs, V3 loss 2.322 vs 2.304, task average 70.1 vs 71.0). Statement 2: its motivation is representation collapse with depth: "the baseline model tends toward representation collapse, characterized by high similarity between features of adjacent layers", and a single stream (n = 1) does not help. Survey use: cite as the origin of the HC mechanism used by Hyperloop; the collapse argument is directly relevant to looped models, whose successive iterations of one block are even more prone to near-identical states, but HC itself was never tested with weight sharing (survey inference). Note memory: n hidden streams per token add activation memory that the paper calls negligible in params/FLOPs, which matters for looped models that already multiply activation memory by loop count. No correction; the survey's design table entry for Hyperloop should cite this paper alongside 2604.21254.

title: The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis
relevance_reason: Two weight-shared passes per token (persistent state step, ephemeral prediction step) along the sequence axis; not depth looping, but the same structure as looped models that keep only the first loop's KV.
one_sentence: Inserts a <predict> step after every token so the input step's KV forms the persistent state while the prediction step's KV is kept only in a short window; from 53M to 1.678B parameters this beats standard Transformers and capacity-matched ablations at matched tokens and GPU-hours.
key_contributions: SPS Transformer: same parameters process each input token (persistent KV) and a following <predict> slot (ephemeral KV, window w = 64) that emits the next token.
Pretraining on FineWeb-Edu at five scales (53M-1.678B, 20B tokens): lowest validation NLL at every scale, 2.3-3.1 point zero-shot gains, same persistent KV size, throughput within 6-10%.
Ablations (2X MEMORY, DELAYED STATE, REVERSE SPS) and gradient analysis show separation, not extra compute or memory, drives the gain; persisting the input stream is the robust choice.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu, 20B tokens by default (STANDARD also trained to 40B for GPU-hour matching)
setup.baselines: STANDARD Transformer, 2X MEMORY, DELAYED STATE, REVERSE SPS (same backbone and parameter count)
setup.benchmarks: FineWeb-Edu validation NLL; WikiText, C4, Pile-Books3, GovReport NLL; ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, PIQA, SciQ, LAMBADA zero-shot

claims.claim: SPS reaches standard-Transformer validation loss with far fewer training tokens; doubling the standard model's token budget does not close the gap.
claims.regime: iso_param; iso_data and matched GPU-hours (STANDARD given 2x tokens)
claims.evidence_quote: At 1.6B parameters, State-Prediction Separation matches the validation loss of a standard Transformer trained on 47B tokens while using 2.6× fewer tokens (pre-decay).

claims.claim: Gains carry to held-out corpora and zero-shot tasks at the same persistent KV footprint and near-equal throughput.
claims.evidence_quote: SPS's persistent KV cache is the same size as S TANDARD's (peak memory ratio 1.01), and end-to-end throughput is within 6–10% of S TANDARD at all scales.

claims.claim: Committing persistent state at the later (prediction) step, which gives the same extra compute without separation, is consistently worse than SPS.
claims.evidence_quote: D ELAYED S TATE does improve over S TANDARD, confirming that the extra computation step carries some benefit, but at every scale SPS remains consistently better, by 0.019–0.021 in validation NLL and by 0.06–0.07 in corpus NLL (Table 2).

claims.claim: Keeping every prediction-step entry persistent (double memory) is worse than SPS with half the persistent cache, so the gain is not capacity-based.
claims.evidence_quote: SPS is consistently better in validation NLL across XS–XL, even though it has half the persistent KV cache. This shows that the gain is not capacity-based.

numbers.what: Zero-shot accuracy gain and OOD corpus NLL drop vs STANDARD
numbers.quote: Corpus NLL on four outof-distribution corpora drops by 0.09–0.11 across scales, and zero-shot accuracy on five standard benchmarks improves by 2.3–3.1%.

numbers.what: Validation NLL gap vs STANDARD from XS to XL
numbers.quote: SPS attains the lowest validation NLL on FineWeb-Edu at every scale, with the gap over S TANDARD widening from −0.042 at XS to −0.068 at XL.

numbers.what: Training-compute overhead
numbers.quote: SPS's prediction stream adds a forward-pass slot per input position, roughly doubling per-step training compute over the standard Transformer;

limitations: Single pretraining corpus; largest scale 1.678B (XL under-trained); each main result from a single run (3-seed check at S); roughly doubles per-step training compute; streams share all parameters.
survey_notes: SECTION: systems (Sec. 8.1, sharing caches) and design space (Sec. 5, state passing / KV sharing across loops). Statement 1: separating a persistent-state pass from an ephemeral prediction pass with shared weights improves LM quality at fixed KV size: "At 1.6B parameters, State-Prediction Separation matches the validation loss of a standard Transformer trained on 47B tokens while using 2.6× fewer tokens", with zero-shot gains of 2.3-3.1% and persistent memory ratio 1.01. Statement 2: which pass persists matters: committing state at the later pass (DELAYED STATE) is worse "by 0.019–0.021 in validation NLL" at equal compute, and doubling persistent memory is also worse ("the gain is not capacity-based"). Survey use: this supplies a mechanism for the surprising Sec. 8 result that the Looped Prediction Transformer's first-recursion-only cache plus a local window 'does not cost quality and instead improves it' (quote from 2610.02383 as used in survey Sec. 8.1) and for PLT/LoopCoder-v2 sharing the first loop's KV: SPS has exactly that structure (persistent first-pass KV, windowed second-pass KV, w = 64), but on the sequence axis. This link is the survey's inference; SPS never mentions looped models. CAVEAT: SPS doubles per-token compute, so its comparison to STANDARD at matched tokens is not compute-matched; the matched-GPU-hours comparison is the fair one. Regime: iso_param + iso_data, plus a GPU-hour-matched comparison. No correction; strong supporting citation for Sec. 8.1 and the design-space state-passing discussion.

title: The Neural Data Router: Adaptive Control Flow in Transformers Improves Systematic Generalization
relevance_reason: Universal-Transformer-style weight-shared layer iterated in depth with a per-column copy gate; extra steps at test time.
one_sentence: Adds a copy gate (skip the whole layer per column, conditioned on attention output) and geometric attention (attend to closest match) to a weight-shared Transformer, reaching 100% length generalization on compositional table lookup and near-perfect depth generalization on arithmetic and ListOps.
key_contributions: Copy gate: sigmoid gate computed from the self-attention output interpolates between the transformed state and the unchanged input, so columns wait until their inputs are ready; bias initialized to -3.
Geometric attention: sigmoid match probabilities combined so each query attends to the closest matching position, giving a locality bias for ordered composition.
Shared-layer depth must match the depth of the computation graph (12 layers generalize on CTL, 10 do not); shared weights allow adding steps at test time (trained 20, tested 24 on ListOps).

setup.model_sizes: small shared-layer Transformer encoders (hyperparameters in paper Table 7)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: CTL (train 1-5 compositions), simple arithmetic (depth up to 5), balanced ListOps (1M training sequences, depth 1-5)
setup.loops_train: depth set to deepest computation path times steps per operation plus a few layers; ListOps trained with 20 layers
setup.loops_test: ListOps tested with 24 layers; CTL test 9-10 compositions
setup.baselines: LSTM, bidirectional LSTM, DNC, Universal Transformer and relative-position variants, +gate and +abs/rel ablations, ACT variants
setup.benchmarks: compositional table lookup (forward/backward), simple arithmetic, balanced ListOps

claims.claim: NDR achieves perfect length generalization on compositional table lookup, which no previous neural network had reported.
claims.regime: unclear (baselines have their own tuned depths)
claims.evidence_quote: Our novel Neural Data Router (NDR) achieves 100% length generalization accuracy on the classic compositional table lookup task, as well as near-perfect accuracy on the simple arithmetic task and a new variant of ListOps testing for generalization across computational depths.

claims.claim: On ListOps, baselines reach near-perfect IID accuracy but fail on deeper test problems, while NDR generalizes.
claims.evidence_quote: Like on the other tasks, the baseline LSTM and Transformers do not generalize well on the test set consisting of deeper problems, while they achieve a near-perfect accuracy on IID data. In contrast, our model achieves near-perfect generalization.

claims.claim: Generalization requires shared-layer depth at least as large as the computation depth.
claims.regime: iso_param (same NDR, varying number of layers)
claims.evidence_quote: We clearly observe that, while the shallow models can also solve the IID split, only the deep models generalize to the longer problems (here the 12-layer model generalizes almost perfectly, but the 10-layer one does not).

claims.claim: Because parameters are shared, more steps can be run at test time than in training without a penalty.
claims.evidence_quote: We did this for the ListOps experiment (Sec. 3.3): the model was trained with 20 layers and tested with 24. Our preliminary experiments confirmed that this practice has no performance penalty, while it speeds up training.

numbers.what: Balanced ListOps IID/test (depth 7-8) accuracy: Transformer, +rel, +abs/rel+gate, NDR
Simple arithmetic generalization test accuracy of NDR
numbers.quote: All considered models perform well on the IID validation data, but none except the NDR performs well on the generalization test set, which achieves near-perfect accuracy of 98%.

numbers.what: Training speed on simple arithmetic
numbers.quote: We also note that the NDR learns very quickly: while all other models require about 200 K steps to converge, the NDR achieves near-perfect accuracy after 50 K steps of training.

limitations: Synthetic algorithmic tasks only; depth must be chosen from the task's computation graph; geometric attention is a strong locality bias; no language modeling.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2022
survey_notes: SECTION: lineage (Sec. 4, 2021-2022 algorithmic UT line; candidate for the timeline table) and design space (Sec. 5, state passing: gating); secondary: theory (Sec. 9.4 length generalization). Statement 1: a gated shared-layer Transformer generalizes across composition depth where ungated ones fail: NDR gets 0.99 on ListOps depth 7-8 vs 0.74 for the Transformer baseline, and "100% length generalization accuracy on the classic compositional table lookup task". Statement 2: depth (number of shared-layer applications) must match the depth of the computation: "the 12-layer model generalizes almost perfectly, but the 10-layer one does not", and shared weights allow running more steps at test time ("the model was trained with 20 layers and tested with 24"; "this practice has no performance penalty"). Survey use: an early, clean instance of two design rules the survey states for looped models: (a) plain residual chaining is insufficient and a learned copy/skip gate conditioned on attention lets columns wait (supports Sec. 5 'Plain chaining is not enough for deep iteration' and the gated-injection option in Sec. 3); (b) loop count must scale with computation depth (consistent with the Sec. 9 statement that positive theorems let loop count grow with input). The paper also reports ACT enabling training of a 14-layer baseline that otherwise failed. MISSING from current survey text (no mention of NDR in lineage or design space).
